title: Why Message Queues
description: Learn why synchronous communication is fragile at scale, and how message queues decouple services for reliability and throughput.

segments.text: Imagine two services talking to each other directly — like a phone call. If one side hangs up, the conversation dies. Today we'll learn why that's a problem and how queues fix it.

Here's Service A calling Service B synchronously. A sends a request, then waits. And waits. A is completely blocked until B responds. They're tightly coupled — like two people on a phone call, both stuck.

Now Service B crashes. What happens to A? It's stuck waiting, eventually times out, and fails too. One service going down cascades into multiple failures. This is the fragility of synchronous communication.
segments.thought_prompt: How could you prevent Service A from failing when Service B goes down?

segments.text: Enter the message queue. Instead of calling B directly, A drops a message into a queue and moves on immediately. It's like leaving a voicemail instead of making a phone call — you don't need the other person to pick up.
Service A is the producer — it creates messages. Service B is the consumer — it reads messages from the queue at its own pace. They don't need to be online at the same time. Beautiful decoupling.

Queues also act as shock absorbers. If a sudden traffic spike produces thousands of messages per second, the queue buffers them. The consumer processes at a steady rate without being overwhelmed. No more dropped requests.

Now, what if multiple services need the same message? That's the pub-sub pattern. One producer publishes to a topic, and multiple subscribers each get a copy. Like a newspaper — one publisher, many readers.
But here's a design question worth pondering. If a consumer crashes after reading a message but before processing it, is that message lost forever?
segments.thought_prompt: How should a queue handle messages when consumers crash mid-processing?

segments.text: Most queues support 'at-least-once' delivery — the message stays in the queue until the consumer acknowledges it. If the consumer crashes, the message gets redelivered. Safe, but your consumer must handle duplicates.

Let's talk about Kafka — the heavyweight of event streaming. Kafka stores messages in partitions within topics. Each partition is an ordered, append-only log. Think of it as a commit log that multiple consumers can read independently.

Kafka's killer feature is consumer groups. Multiple consumers in a group split the partitions between them for parallel processing. If one consumer dies, its partitions are reassigned to survivors. Automatic load balancing and fault tolerance.

So: synchronous calls couple services tightly. Queues decouple them. Pub-sub fans out to many consumers. Kafka gives you durable, partitioned, replayable event streams. Async communication is the backbone of resilient distributed systems.
